analysis.one_liner: Bars federal agencies from regulating tobacco or tobacco ads in motorsports and strips the FDA of tobacco authority.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a vote before Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar the Health and Human Services Secretary and every other federal agency from regulating how NASCAR and other racing organizations use or promote tobacco, and from acting against tobacco advertising in racing. Its final section goes much further: it declares that no law can give the Food and Drug Administration any authority to regulate tobacco products at all. So while the bill is framed around stock car racing, it would permanently remove all federal tobacco regulation.
analysis.who_benefits: Tobacco manufacturers, whose racing sponsorships (a major marketing channel) would be shielded from any federal rule, and who would be insulated from FDA oversight of tobacco generally. Racing organizations that depend on tobacco sponsorship money also gain.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Tobacco companies and racing series sponsors

how_it_helps.text: It prohibits any federal official from regulating the promotion or use of tobacco by NASCAR or any other professional motorsports association under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, the Federal Cigarette Labeling and Advertising Act, and the Comprehensive Smokeless Tobacco Health Education Act of 1986 [S3][S2].

Its final section states that nothing in this or any other law may give the FDA any authority to regulate tobacco or tobacco products in any manner — eliminating the legal basis for the FDA's 1990s effort to regulate cigarettes [S3][S2].
It also bars enforcement of any executive order touching tobacco use or advertising in motorsports, and preserves only state laws banning tobacco sales to people under 18 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people, who would bear the health costs of keeping cigarette and smokeless tobacco marketing shielded from federal regulation — including advertising aimed at the large audiences motorsports events attract.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, through preventable tobacco harm

drawbacks.text: The bill is far broader than its racing framing: Section 3 would strip the FDA of all authority over tobacco for everyone, not just motorsports, so the public-health cost would reach well beyond race fans [S3][S2].
It would block even executive orders in this area, removing a tool future administrations could use to address tobacco marketing, while leaving states able to act only on sales to minors [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits flow almost entirely to tobacco manufacturers and their sponsored racing series, while its costs — weakened federal authority over a product that causes cancer and nicotine addiction — fall on the public. There is essentially no offsetting public benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the 104th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jesse Helms introduced the bill on September 29, 1995, joined by Sens. Faircloth and Warner; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S1][S3][S5].
The cosponsor list shows 3 Republicans, and no committee hearing, markup, floor vote, or any further action appears in the record [S4][S5].
Congress ended on January 3, 1997 without the bill receiving a vote in either chamber [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people and public health: because the bill died in committee, no carve-out was enacted and no law was changed to bar federal agencies from regulating tobacco. Tobacco manufacturers and racing sponsors gained nothing from the bill's failure to advance — they simply kept the status quo they already had.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public; no tobacco carve-out was enacted

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the sponsor and all 3 cosponsors were Republicans, several from tobacco-growing states, so the bill's visible support was entirely Republican.

industries.note: The bill would have exempted tobacco marketing in motorsports from federal regulation and, through its final section, eliminated all FDA authority over tobacco. That protects a marketing channel that puts cigarette branding in front of millions of fans, at the public's health expense.

industries.industry: Professional motorsports (NASCAR and other racing series)
industries.note: The bill would lock in tobacco sponsorship revenue for racing organizations, which historically was a major funding source tied to on-track cigarette and smokeless tobacco advertising.
